subject: Career
title: Connectors, Mavens, and Salesmen
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Connectors, Mavens, and Salesmen.

hook.text: Some people seem to know everyone. Malcolm Gladwell calls them Connectors.

buildup.text: In 'The Tipping Point,' Gladwell identifies three social roles: Connectors, Mavens, and Salesmen.

discovery.text: Connectors link groups. Mavens gather and share knowledge. Salesmen persuade people to act.

twist.text: You don't have to be all three. But knowing one of each in your network multiplies your reach.

climax.text: Identify which role comes naturally to you and lean into it. Then befriend the other types.

punchline.text: Know who connects, who knows, and who convinces.

quiz.question: What are Gladwell's three social roles in The Tipping Point?

details.summary: Malcolm Gladwell's The Tipping Point identifies three social archetypes: Connectors who know many people, Mavens who accumulate and share knowledge, and Salesmen who persuade others. Career networkers benefit from understanding which archetype they embody.
details.whyItMatters: Knowing your natural networking archetype lets you play to your strengths rather than forcing an unnatural style, making your networking efforts more authentic and effective.
takeaways: Connectors thrive on introducing people across diverse groups
Mavens build influence through expertise and information sharing
Most effective networkers combine elements of all three archetypes

faq.question: Which of Gladwell's three archetypes is most valuable for career advancement?
faq.answer: Each offers distinct advantages. Connectors gain access and opportunities. Mavens become trusted authorities. Salesmen influence decisions. For career advancement specifically, the Connector archetype creates the most direct path to opportunities through sheer volume of relationships.

faq.question: Can you develop traits of an archetype that does not come naturally?
faq.answer: Yes, with practice. An introvert who is naturally a Maven can develop Connector habits by setting small goals like attending one event monthly. The archetypes are tendencies, not fixed identities, and can be deliberately expanded.
